title: Argentina's bid to stop Falkland Islands oil drilling rejected
html:
• Published

Argentina's bid to block an oil exploration project near the Falkland Islands has been rejected by a UN-backed international tribunal.

The Argentinian government had called for the venture to be blocked as it claimed there was an ongoing dispute over the sovereignty of the Falklands, a British overseas territory. The UK has repeatedly rejected Argentina's claim.

In a decision on Saturday, the court's president said there did not appear to be any basis for believing it had jurisdiction as the tribunal is unable to rule on questions of sovereignty.

In a vote 18 to 3, judges from the International Tribunal for the Law of the Sea rejected Argentina's challenge.

The Sea Lion oilfield, around 130 miles (209 km) from the Falkland Islands, contains an estimated 1.7 billion barrels of oil.

Two oil companies – Britain's Rockhopper Exploration and Israel's Navitas Petroleum – are due to begin extracting from the oilfield within two years, potentially generating huge revenues for the roughly 3,500 inhabitants of the islands.

But the Argentinian government claimed the marine environment of disputed maritime areas is protected by international law.

In a 2013 referendum, residents of the islands voted overwhelmingly to remain a British overseas territory - with 99.8% voting in favour and just three voting against.

Argentine forces landed on the Falklands to stake a territorial claim in 1982, sparking a 74-day war over the territory as a British military task force ejected them.

The conflict led to the deaths of 255 British military personnel, three islanders and 649 Argentine military personnel.
summary: A joint venture between UK-Israeli companies is set to start exploring for oil and gas, but Argentina sought to block it as part of its claim to sovereignty.
